entries.title: Why Does Donald Trump Hate This Sculpture?
entries.summary: The president wants the Smithsonian to add a colossal George Washington statue—and remove another work of abstract art in D.C.
entries.content:
The president wants the Smithsonian to add a colossal George Washington statue—and remove another work of abstract art in D.C.

The sculpture that Donald Trump wants removed from the National Mall has a reputation even among its admirers for being a bit inscrutable. Dedicated in 1967 at what is now the National Museum of American History, José de Rivera’s Infinity looks, fittingly, like an infinity symbol with an extra twist. (A bow? A pretzel?) By pairing the technical prowess required to create smooth, curved metal with the delicate spinning of a music box, the slow-turning work seems to take a different form each time you pass it. The museum’s architect, Walker O. Cain, wrote that Infinity “has the characteristic of stimulating everyone who has seen it to create his own personal imaginative interpretation.”

But the president does not appear to have been stimulated. “That strange modernist sculpture tells visitors nothing about America, inspires no one, and honors none of our Great American Heroes,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Friday night. Trump insisted that the Smithsonian replace Infinity with a 30-foot high “Colossus” of George Washington. In the same post, he called for the mounting of a five-year exhibition about the Founding Father to open immediately (museum shows of such magnitude typically take years to plan), and said the museum should create a “Center for American Heroes.” Trump also wrote that the institution should add another, 11-foot-tall Washington statue to the museum’s Flag Hall. That one was displayed at the Grand Prix race held in Washington, D.C., this summer as part of Trump’s Freedom 250 festivities. He’d like it dedicated at the museum this Thursday.

Trump’s latest demands might be partially understood as a test of how far he can push an institution that he does not control. They came just three days after the Smithsonian’s secretary, Lonnie Bunch, announced his upcoming retirement, following a year and a half of standing between the museum complex and the White House. In a July executive order, the president called on the National Park Service, which is part of the executive branch, to place signs outside the National Museum of American History accusing it of partisan bias.

Few would question the appropriateness of having a healthy amount of George Washington in an American-history museum, but Trump’s ask might be a little too redundant. For one thing, a Washington sculpture can already be found on the museum’s second floor. Classical in style and portraying the first president as a kind of Zeus figure, Horatio Greenough’s 1841 statue boasts chiseled muscles that rival even the machismo AI depictions Trump circulates of himself and Washington online. And when approached from the east, Rivera’s Infinity—the aspirational site of Trump’s Washington colossus—elegantly frames another abstract form: the obelisk known as the Washington Monument.

Trump’s call for changes to the museum fits a few recent patterns: He has been on a campaign to institute his preferred version of history in the national museum system. He has begun to leave his mark, and occasionally his name, across the architectural landscape of Washington, D.C. And while doing so, he appears to have indicated a distaste for abstract art. Earlier this month, the Kennedy Center, which Trump controls, took down Joel Shapiro’s playful metal sculpture Blue. When the Trump administration—addressing a controversy at the National Portrait Gallery last year—criticized a decidedly representational Amy Sherald painting of a trans woman as Lady Liberty, part of its complaint was that, in the words of the administration, “the Statue of Liberty is not an abstract canvas for political expression.” The use of abstract reads like an insult.

Trump has pushed a classical makeover in D.C.. He has issued executive orders mandating classical designs as the default for new federal buildings, for example, and remounted figurative statues that were torn down during the Black Lives Matter movement. He has mused about the White House upgrading its columns to a higher Greek order (adding more classical to the neoclassical); his most prized project, the White House ballroom, looks like a Corinthian-columned department store. In his first executive order on architecture, he said federal buildings should command respect.

When it comes to the Rivera outside the National Museum of American History, Trump’s issue with it—and with abstraction largely—might not be that the sculpture “says nothing about America,” but that it doesn’t say what he wants it to. That is, he can’t control what it says at all.

The American artist Robert Motherwell wrote in a 1951 essay celebrating abstraction that one of the most striking aspects of the approach is its “nakedness,” or the way it turns, with such decisiveness, away from the symbols we know. “How many rejections on the part of her artists! Whole worlds—the world of objects, the world of power and propaganda, the world of anecdotes, the world of fetishes and ancestor worship,” he wrote. With abstract works such as Infinity, we’re free to find our own reading—or not.

Whereas abstraction attempts to reject passed-down meanings, the image of George Washington is layered with them. Part of what is so moving about, say, getting up close to Washington’s military uniform at the National Museum of American History is the way it challenges how we’ve come to see him as an icon rather than as an actual person.

Abstraction has long been subject to right-wing attacks. During the Red Scare, for instance, George A. Dondero, a U.S. representative from Michigan, crusaded to rid American art of what he saw as communist influence. In a 1949 speech that could be ripped from Truth Social today, he framed a list of 20th-century art movements as un-American weapons for destruction: “Dadaism aims to destroy by ridicule. Expressionism aims to destroy by aping the primitive and insane,” he said. “Abstractionism aims to destroy by the creation of brainstorms.”

Sure, the unpredictable responses to abstract art—the brainstorms—can be a little intimidating. How many of us have stood, a bit clueless, before Jackson Pollock’s riotous colors or Cy Twombly’s frenetic scratches and wondered if we might need a Ph.D. for this?

But there’s also a certain joy to find in it. One National Museum of American History curator, David Shayt, embraced the compounding, shifting meanings of abstraction in a 2008 essay about the museum’s Rivera. The sculpture marked an early work of abstract art commissioned by the U.S. government, but, Shayt argues, the commission was more about the government’s belief that Rivera, a prominent abstract-expressionist sculptor known for his twisting metal forms, could capture the museum’s dual identity in its early days as the National Museum of History and Technology. Cain, the architect, had convinced the government that the sculpture would be a mechanical model of the solar system, a “twenty-first-century orrery.” But Rivera, who cited the abstractionist Piet Mondrian and the sculptor Constantin Brâncuși as among his influences, asserted no such thing. “What I make represents nothing but itself,” he said.

That didn’t stop the National Museum of American History’s staff from making their own meaning over the years, particularly as employees of a “pragmatic museum of history rather than a museum of art,” Shayt wrote. “Is it a mathematical symbol? A wisp of battlefield smoke? A tennis stroke?” he asked of Infinity. One of the sculpture’s greatest attributes, he continued, is “an expressiveness that can evolve in step with the evolution of the museum whose entrance it fronts.”

For an example of the kind of aesthetic Trump prefers, you don’t have to go far from the Rivera. A short walk brings you to Freedom Plaza, where the National Park Service has installed a pop-up exhibition for the nation’s 250th birthday. Rows of traditional, metal statues of Revolutionary War soldiers line the plaza—many, notably, represent enslaved individuals. Standing on a high plinth, meanwhile, is Caesar Rodney, a slaveholder and Declaration of Independence signer, who looms over the display. The statue had been removed in Delaware during the Black Lives Matter protests, only to be restored in Washington as some conservatives began championing him as a symbol of the left’s overreach. Trump has placed a similar style of traditional statue—direct, simple—throughout the White House Rose Garden and envisions much of the same for the Garden of American Heroes, another of his planned D.C. projects, where abstraction is explicitly forbidden. There’s very little room for interpretation in these sorts of statues. They mean what they mean.

Much of the Trump-era fight over history has boiled down to a struggle about trust. The Trump administration says the history the Smithsonian tells is not patriotic enough; the institution counters that Americans can hold patriotism and complexity at once. The National Museum of American History museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, told a congressional committee this summer: “Telling our history fully is not anti-American. It is a form of respect for the American people.” Abstraction, too, holds a kind of esteem for its viewers, trusting them to navigate its symbol-less terrain. In his essay, Motherwell wrote that the emergence of abstract art is one sign that there are still people who “know how to respect and follow their inner feelings, no matter how irrational or absurd they may first appear.”

On the west side of the museum stands another abstract piece, a massive, 40-foot Alexander Calder that the museum calls a “monument to modernity.” Its jagged black edges reach outward, conveying a sense of rupture or change. On Saturday, the area around the Calder was roped off with caution tape, surely something to do with conservation or work on the museum grounds. But it felt a little ominous, as though it were a warning not for museumgoers, but for the art itself.

entries.title: A Nation of Strange, Idle Men
entries.summary: Jon Ronson’s The Castle argues that men are giving up on society because they have nothing better to do.
entries.content:
Jon Ronson’s The Castle argues that men are giving up on society because they have nothing better to do.

Like many Millennial men, I used to be pretty invested in Ye, the artist formerly known as Kanye West—primarily because of his music, but also because of his unique position as the one celebrity who seemed empowered to behave however he wanted. He interrupted Taylor Swift at the Video Music Awards; he said “George Bush doesn’t care about Black people” at a Hurricane Katrina fundraiser; he brought a Jesus look-alike onstage. I would shrug, and keep listening. Then his do what I want ethos went very bad. Ye called slavery “a choice”; he came out as a fan of Hitler; he wore a KKK-style hood.

With escalating horror, I questioned what had happened. Was it about having too much money? Untreated mental illness? I wondered when logic and shame might kick in—when someone might get him to stop. But the more he was rejected by his peers, the media, and some fans, the more Kanye seemed to act out. Eventually, I accepted, grimly, that I was watching someone who, feeling abandoned and misunderstood, was determined to ignore all of his critics and double down on pursuing his chosen path.

I thought about Ye while I was reading The Castle, a new nonfiction work by the journalist Jon Ronson that attempts to unpack the motivations of wayward men who no longer fit into traditional society. Ronson is probably best-known for his 2015 book, So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed, a journalistic account of the emotional incentives and historical context behind the social-media-fueled frenzy that became known as “cancel culture.” Like the people in that book, many of the subjects of The Castle have been shoved to the margins. But the forces at play in this new book are more disparate, and perhaps more stubborn, than an angry online mob. Ronson explores how men become alienated because they can’t achieve success in their chosen field, because they can’t pay their bills, because they have too much money, because the town around them went to hell. The book shows how their free will, coupled with a lot of free time on the internet, leads them to pursue their self-interest as best they can—which, eventually, begets more alienation.

The Castle opens with the story of a strange encounter with a strange man. One night in 2023, Ronson’s 20-something son, Joel, and three of his friends (two are women) are invited to a mysterious castle in the middle of nowhere—specifically, Woodstock, Connecticut—for what they believe is a party. There, the women are asked to participate in a bizarre dating show hosted by a man named Chris Mark. The idea is apparently that 101 women will dress up like princesses and vie to be Mark’s girlfriend; once the situation becomes predictably awkward, Mark seemingly deems the night a bust and kicks everyone out. Ronson, who wakes up to a slew of texts from Joel describing what happened, is alarmed by the whole episode—and decides he needs to meet Mark himself.

On their first meeting, Mark at first seems transparent about how he spends his time. He owns the castle, where he lives with several women who he met online. The entire scene strikes Ronson as reminiscent of Hugh Hefner’s grotto—an analogy they discuss at Ronson’s prompting. But Mark, in Ronson’s telling, quickly grows antagonistic, abruptly asking Ronson to sign an NDA, then later barraging him with suspicious texts and threatening him with a pair of goons. Ronson concludes that Mark has “nurtured a private fantasy of manhood” that the journalist has put at risk by asking questions. (Mark has contested many of the details and claims of The Castle, including that he sent anyone to threaten Ronson, and has said that Ronson “presented me and events involving me in a profoundly misleading manner.”)

The Castle is about both Ronson’s investigation into Mark and the bigger phenomenon Mark seems to represent: too-idle men, most of them less wealthy than Mark, littering the country, yearning for some kind of grander purpose. He’s especially interested in men ages 25 to 54 who are both unemployed and no longer looking for work—people he claims have “opted out of society,” choosing instead a “life of male nothingness.” In a moment of general anxiety about men—whom they vote for, what they’re reading, whether they share their feelings—his interest isn’t political. It’s empathic. He offers no prescriptive solutions, wags no fingers. Instead, he wants the reader to conceive of the scale of social anomie, and to envision the millions of other men chasing meaning in the wreckage of their former aspirations.

In particular, Ronson focuses on a demographic whose life expectancy has dropped in the 21st century: middle-aged white men without college degrees, many of whom suffer from what a pair of Princeton economists he speaks with define as “deaths of despair” brought on by “the erosion of a way of life.” Once upon a time, such men—who widely supported Donald Trump in all three of his runs for president—were sold on the American dream. Now some of them are characterized by “a kind of cowed, vaguely shocked hopelessness,” Ronson writes. Others, facing social rejection, have started to live “like separatists, creating worlds in which they didn’t have to live or interact with other people except on their own terms.” Women, too, suffer from deaths of despair—but it’s the men, Ronson indicates, who have been raised to envision themselves as heroes, a self-image that can drive them to dark places.

Ronson illustrates how easy it can be for these men to slide off the map. His most endearing subject is Greg Chism, a father of two daughters in small-town Illinois. Chism was a single parent with tons of medical debt living in a place without a lot of job opportunities when, in the 2010s, he discovered a YouTube channel encouraging viewers to “make a video and change your life.” A few of his early videos got some attention, after which Chism received coaching from the platform’s employees, and he eventually struck on a winning formula: bizarre sketches involving his two daughters that played like the output of a hallucinating LLM fed on Nickelodeon. These generated millions of views, and some of them got really weird; Chism and his kids dressed like babies, or pretended to eat cat food off pizza. Soon came the blowback: Chism was, the internet claimed, a bad father abusing his children by making them participate in these creepy videos. His channel was demonetized, then banned. He was shunned just as quickly as he’d been celebrated.

But Chism, whom Ronson tracks down, has not been radicalized by the wave of hatred that came his way. Nor does he seem to be a bad father; his (now teenage) kids express mostly fond memories of their channel. He admits making errors in judgment—see: cat food—but in the end, Ronson writes, Chism was “a single father juggling responsibilities while feeling foolishly idealistic about sharing his family’s lives on the internet.” Becoming a YouTuber had seemed like a way for Chism to stop sliding toward destitution. Instead, his entire life was put under a microscope. Ronson uses Chism’s guilelessness to show how unexpected and profound the pitfalls can be for anyone looking to find a foothold in the new world.

So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed examined a group of people whose lives were ruined by the internet in one particular way; The Castle flips the framing. In the latter book’s view, the internet allows its users to choose their own particular off-ramp from ennui. Seeking female companionship, Chris Mark turns to dating apps; eager to feel seen, Greg Chism becomes a YouTuber. One subject, the podcaster Andrew Gold, begins tailoring his content to anti-woke audiences, racking up huge numbers by playing to the preexisting grievances of his angry followers. Another chapter digs into Ronson’s rocky friendship with the comedy writer Graham Linehan, whose involvement in the gender-critical movement led him to act out online in ways that Ronson reads as self-destructive. (Linehan has disputed many of the details of Ronson’s depiction, and called it “an indictment of him and the cowardly, careerist, mendacious class of people who could roughly gather under the title ‘Graham Linehan’s old friends and colleagues.’”)

A swerve comes toward the end when Ronson wonders whether he has fallen into the same trap as some of those men. By treating Mark’s story as something only he can make sense of, Ronson has neglected his friends and his marriage. “Everyone I met for this book had, I thought, a similarly dysfunctional relationship with purpose, hunting too desperately for it,” he writes. “And now there was a generation of men, unanchored from society and going it alone—as content creators, culture war influencers, amateur sleuths.”

Ronson doesn’t build toward any prescriptive conclusions; he gives these men a platform to explain how they feel, and allows the reader to weigh the validity of those feelings. I remember the Chism pile-on well, and was slightly horrified to hear the story from his perspective—how confusing it must have felt to toggle so rapidly and randomly between being seen as heroic and villainous. Ronson’s empathy is not boundless; he draws hard lines around some of Mark’s behavior. But he seems to understand that his personal judgment is more or less meaningless. The factors shaping these men are external, but how they react comes from the inside—and many of them remain trapped in their own metaphorical castles, far from the light.

entries.title: Americans Don’t Understand Who’s Rich
entries.summary: The small-business owners with curiously large fortunes
entries.content:
Terry Taylor is worth about $2 billion, and you have almost surely never heard of him. Based in Florida, he doesn’t put his name on the car dealerships that he buys up, and he reportedly attends conferences only on the condition that no one announces who he is. Taylor came to our attention in 2023, when he paid $76 million for an Aspen mansion—then the most expensive home sale in the Colorado town’s history.

In 2024, Forbes magazine, which keeps tabs on the richest people in the United States and around the world, slotted Taylor in at No. 1,694 on its World Billionaires List and published a profile titled “The Car Dealership Billionaire No One Knows.” “He’s like Batman,” a source told Forbes. “You hear about him and you admire his work, but nobody has really ever seen him in real life.”

When Americans picture the ultrarich, they typically think of tech billionaires such as Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, whose wealth lies predominantly in shares of publicly traded companies. They might also think of Wall Street financiers and celebrities such as Taylor Swift. But far more typical are figures like Terry Taylor—which is to say, owners of successful privately held businesses. We are economists who have been studying taxation and inequality for more than a decade. By our calculations, about 1.7 million Americans have each built a net worth of at least $10 million by owning a private business. For every CEO of a public company, there are more than 1,000 private-business owners with a net worth of more than $25 million.

In the course of our research, we’ve come to call these people “everywhere millionaires” because they exist all around the country, in a huge range of industries. Perhaps not surprising, some of these millionaires have stakes in investment firms or medical, dental, or legal practices. But the ranks of everywhere millionaires also include a repo man from Henderson, Nevada; a car-wash owner from Milwaukee; a treated-lumber magnate from Alabama; a boat-cover maker from the Ozarks.

What we found changed how we think about inequality. During the Occupy Wall Street protests after the 2008 financial crisis, the prototypical one-percenters were executives at big banks. Today, when Senators Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders propose making the rich pay their fair share, they aim at Wall Street and Silicon Valley. But far more relevant to the story of inequality in America are the everywhere millionaires who quietly press their elected representatives for favorable treatment. The tax code bears their imprint far more than it does Musk’s.

Last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, for example, gutted the electric-vehicle and clean-energy credits, to the Tesla CEO’s detriment. The same bill made permanent a 20 percent deduction that effectively lowers the top tax rate for private-business owners from 37 percent to 30 percent. And it preserved a loophole that lets business owners in most of the country, but not salaried employees, deduct their state and local taxes in full.

When asked on Meet the Press why the cut for the highest earners had to be permanent, House Speaker Mike Johnson said: “This is not giving tax cuts to millionaires; it’s the opposite. The people in the tax bracket that you’re referring to, many of them are small-business owners.” Although many top-bracket taxpayers do indeed own businesses, the benefits of these provisions flow overwhelmingly to the wealthiest among them.

A loophole that lets private-business owners avoid Medicare taxes has similarly been justified as a break for the little guy. Preserving the family farm has been a pretext for passing ever larger exemptions to the estate tax, to the point that a married couple can now pass on $30 million to heirs tax-free. Hiding behind small business, in short, has proved a devastatingly effective strategy for the rich.

The financial affairs of some of the wealthiest Americans have long been opaque. The Forbes 400 began in 1982 at the direction of the publisher Malcolm Forbes, who reportedly had been inspired by the ballroom capacity at the New York socialite Caroline Astor’s Fifth Avenue mansion. At the time, editorial staffers doubted they could find the 400 richest people, let alone measure their wealth. Although for public companies, people who own a large number of shares must disclose their holdings, and the compensation of top executives is a matter of public record, many wealthy owners of privately held businesses closely guard details about their finances. Kerry Dolan, a Forbes editor, told The New York Times in 2022 that the magazine’s search for billionaires might never pick up on someone who had quietly made $250 million from selling a stake in a business and had invested the proceeds well.

The U.S. government’s view into this world is similarly limited. The Federal Reserve’s Survey of Consumer Finances includes a supplemental sample of a few hundred ultrarich respondents. Tracking down even this small number of people requires an expert staff to conduct interviews and a budget of tens of millions of dollars, a survey official told us. Only one in 10 who are contacted cooperates with the survey. The IRS collects voluminous confidential information about businesses and their owners. But it’s stored in a labyrinth of separate systems and databases, making it hard for anyone to use it to answer even basic questions: How many private-business owners are there across the United States? How rich are they, and how did they become rich? Without detailed information on how privately held businesses operate and make money, experts cannot estimate the effects of tax changes and other policies.

After the two of us finished graduate school in 2014, we worked as unpaid analysts for the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Tax Analysis. Along with our friend Danny Yagan, we were assigned a project to help the department figure out how much tax various categories of business owners were paying, and we were given a database of anonymized records to analyze. (For research purposes, each taxpayer is assigned a unique identification number. The names and actual tax IDs of the businesses and individuals who submit tax forms are confidential; the IRS cannot legally disclose them even to other parts of the government.) By combining various data sets over the course of months, we could fill out a detailed map of American enterprise and observe how business owners build their fortunes.

Even without knowing owners’ names, we learned a lot: We were able to cross-reference the tax data with anonymized data sets from past research containing standardized-test scores, parental income, and early-career trajectories. This information became the statistical foundation for a series of research papers.

The more we came to recognize the importance of everywhere millionaires, the more we wanted to understand their decision making. So we sought to identify some through public sources and tell their stories. We looked, for instance, at trade publications that ranked top earners. We interviewed industry experts and combed through databases such as Dun & Bradstreet, which collects reams of information about businesses and their leaders. We also tapped our own networks.

The more people we told about our quest to find rich private-business owners, the more leads we gathered. A family member from St. Louis pointed us to the Tracy family, who owns Dot Foods—the nation’s largest food redistributor, which generates more than $10 billion in revenue a year and was started from the back of a station wagon by a dairy farmer and his wife, Dorothy, in rural Illinois. Some of the most memorable businesses we came across were the least glamorous. One was a regional distributor of garbage trucks, street sweepers, and sewer suckers for municipalities.

Once we identified the top earners in an industry, we learned more about them through public information, such as newspaper and magazine profiles and published memoirs. Property records for luxury homes and registries of private-jet and yacht owners pointed us to colorful stories. We traced a 100-foot yacht moored off Manhattan Beach to the founder of Bird Barrier, a company that keeps pigeons off buildings. A 383-foot yacht belonged to the man who built Harbor Freight Tools, the discount-tool chain. Others were owned by a forklift manufacturer in New Bremen, Ohio; a Long Island scrap-metal recycler; and a slew of auto dealers.

Whatever they sell—cars, treated lumber, boat covers—the everywhere millionaires have one thing in common: They own what have become known as pass-through businesses because their profits skip the traditional corporate tax entirely and flow straight to owners, to be taxed at the individual rate. This structure surged in popularity following the Tax Reform Act of 1986, which cut the top individual tax rate to less than the corporate tax rate for the first time in U.S. history. In the decades since, lawmakers have carved out multiple loopholes, so a dollar earned from owning a business is routinely taxed much less than a dollar earned in wages. Moreover, business owners have a far greater ability to underreport their income to the IRS than wealthy CEOs do.

In some sense, getting rich by starting a business is an old American story, but the rise of education-dependent knowledge industries has gotten much more attention in the past few decades. When we were graduating from college, we were drawn to what many American middle-class families have come to see as the conventional paths to prosperity: tech and finance. Eric worked for a time as a software developer in a few start-ups, and Owen as an analyst at a venture-capital firm. But our subsequent economic research showed that studying, going to good schools, and then landing a job working at a prestigious company was hardly the only way to get ahead.

In the upper reaches of the wealth distribution, the advantages of entrepreneurship appear stark. According to our analysis of the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, the 65,000 American households worth more than $100 million consisted almost entirely of business owners; fewer than half held graduate degrees. When we matched entrepreneurs with their test scores, we found that people with average SAT results were more likely to build a highly successful business than to make a comparable fortune as a salaried worker. Owning, it turns out, often beats earning.

But for all the benefits of entrepreneurial risk-taking, everywhere millionaires are also the beneficiaries of U.S. government policy, which they shape to their advantage.

As Congress drafted the 2017 tax law—which ultimately became the biggest business-tax cut in history—we met an auto dealer who had become a member of Congress and warned that the bill would devastate his industry. Dealers borrow heavily to keep cars on the lot. To help offset the tax cuts, the proposed bill limited how much interest businesses could deduct. By the time the bill passed, though, auto dealers had won a special exemption from that limit.

Once you start watching for favors like this, you see these business owners’ influence everywhere: in tax legislation, in market regulation (or the lack thereof), and in the backgrounds of candidates for elected office. Everywhere millionaires don’t get the same attention as eccentric tech titans, finance executives, or famous entertainers. But seeing them is the first step to understanding the economy and society as they really are.

entries.content:
In The Atlantic’s October cover story, “Empire of Grift,” staff writer Anne Applebaum examines how far-right ideologues have transformed American foreign policy into a tool of private gain and antidemocratic reaction. Instead of making the world safe for democracy, she writes, U.S. foreign policy is rewiring the international order.



Reporting from Brazil, Applebaum reveals that the United States is not the ally Brazilians once knew. No longer is American power deployed solely by trained diplomats and reliable officials, working through state channels; instead, “informal envoys, private companies, online grifters, and hardened ideologues both inside and outside the government matter more. Unlike their predecessors, these people do not talk about spreading democracy, and don’t want to build long-term relationships. They don’t care about America’s reputation. They are deploying the tools of American diplomacy and government for their own purposes, to promote their own business interests or their own ideological goals, because, suddenly, they can.”



Though the Trumpists currently in charge of the U.S. federal government are frequently described as “isolationists,” Applebaum argues that that characterization is wrong. Many of these officials “don’t think of themselves as ordinary Republicans who won an election and will temporarily hold power until the next election. Nor are they mere appendages of Trump. They believe they represent something much greater: the vanguard of a movement that will alter not just America, but the world.”



Applebaum continues, “Like earlier revolutionaries, they do not believe that their opponents are legitimate rivals … Their enemies are existential, and they are international: super-spreaders of a ‘wokeness’ plague, or proponents of a fictitious ‘censorship-industrial complex,’ or advocates of ‘regulation’ that will hamper American business, or self-hating promoters of ‘mass migration’ who want to drown Western civilization in a sea of brown-faced aliens. To maintain their power and defeat these enemies, the predators, like their Bolshevik counterparts, cannot rely on traditional diplomacy, because they don’t trust its practitioners.”



The democratic world that came into being after 1945—a world based not exclusively on law, but on a set of mostly self-imposed restraints—is changing, Applebaum writes. In the post-1945 democratic order, Applebaum observes, “American power was largely derived from alliances that it refrained from exploiting. Long-term relationships were held to be valuable, because you never knew when you might need your allies.” That U.S.-led democratic order was of enormous benefit to this country and to the world: “America helped build eight decades of peace, prosperity, and eventually democracy in Europe and much of Asia, creating markets for U.S. companies and unprecedented support for U.S. power. This world is fast disappearing. Instead, following the president’s lead, different people inside and outside the administration are seizing the revolutionary moment in order to win zero-sum victories. Countries that hang back from this free-for-all know they will suffer. ‘If we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu,’ Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said at Davos earlier this year. He was right.”



Anne Applebaum’s “Empire of Grift” was published today at TheAtlantic.com. Please reach out with any questions or requests.

entries.title: George Lucas’s Next Great Epic Is an Art Museum
entries.summary: Inside the Star Wars creator’s temple to storytelling
entries.content:
Inside the Star Wars creator’s temple to storytelling

What’s your story? The story that you live by, that your cells are geared to, even or especially when you’re not thinking about it? Do we create our own meaning, or should we be trying to discover the meaning that created us? Is it the tractor beams of heavenly love that hold us here, like God’s guy ropes, or are we adrift?

When George Lucas, a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, began writing the screenplay for Star Wars, he had a copy of Joseph Campbell’s The Hero With a Thousand Faces clamped, so to speak, between his teeth. For Campbell, a professor with a popular touch, life was nothing more or less than a summons to greatness. Across cultures, and across the history of the human imagination, he had discerned it, “the one, shape-shifting yet marvelously constant story”: the hero’s journey. Departure, initiation, return. Living is a heroic business, Campbell insisted. Stacked with trials, sure, and frightful reversals, but with the grail floating always ahead of us, calling us onward. Use the Force, Luke. Let go!

And now Lucas has built a temple to story. The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, which opens this month in Exposition Park, just south of downtown Los Angeles, is a swooping, brain-beggaring, super-sexy, twin-bodied leviathan of a megastructure, white as the gown of Princess Leia, half spaceship, half cetacean, all curves, Shangri-la for skateboarders if they could ever get inside. Co-founded by Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson, it hoists itself into twinkling California emptiness on an 11-acre site (formerly two parking lots) next to the Natural History Museum and the L.A. Memorial Coliseum. Walking toward it, you think: Jesus. Eighth wonder? Squillion-dollar folly? Architectural embodiment of some impulse from spiritus mundi? Entering it, you stop thinking altogether. As I passed from the dreamy light of the covered forecourt, a single lens-like portal in its ceiling (for maximum diffraction of heavenly tractor beams), and into the space-gobbling atrium, I was conscious only of a delighted vertigo. Like, awe. Like, wow.

It was an old-school encounter with the sublime, not unlike the one I’d had as a 9-year-old, in 1977, in a cinema in Cambridge, England, watching the first scene of Star Wars. You remember the first scene of Star Wars. A tiny fleeing Rebel ship zips past us into the star-pricked abyss, laser bolts pinging around it, and then, and then, Darth Vader’s Star Destroyer drones overhead, shears off the top of the screen, the viewer’s eye hauled powerless and silently wow-ing for what feels like miles along the faceted grayness of its Imperial underbelly. Agog in my cinema seat, I was a tiny, grubby Shelley, and before me was Mont Blanc.

Lucas and Hobson thought about building their museum in San Francisco; there were prolonged negotiations to build it in Chicago; but it’s landed in the right place: fictive L.A., the Kingdom of Story, where even now, in coffee shops and one-room apartments across the city, on laptops sweating with hope, at least 400 screenplays are being written in accordance with the immemorial template mapped out by Campbell and industrialized by Lucas. Look around: Everyone here is on their hero’s journey.

So in Exposition Park it sublimely squats, the Lucas Museum, flaring its contours into the L.A. void. Why is it so bloody enormous? Because it has to be. Because larger and grander and deeper than the campus itself—with its library, two movie theaters, 100,000 square feet of gallery space, and sculpted stretch of public parkland—is the wobbling master-idea of Lucas himself: a museum of narrative art. Of images that tell or contain or project or smell like a story.

Which means … pretty much everything in the history of art that isn’t abstract. Which means the story of art itself, from the hovering aurochs and Paleolithic handprints of the cave paintings of Altamira (presented here in a glowing full-size reproduction) to the gods-and-monsters heavy-metal dream time of Paul Raymond Gregory. Which means comics, murals, film, Conan the Barbarian and Frida Kahlo, Andrea Solario’s Salome With the Head of John the Baptist and Robert Crumb’s Book of Genesis. (First frame: God holding a big old hairy ball of Chaos in his hands.) Which means Richard Ansdell’s The Death of Sir William Lambton at the Battle of Marston Moor next to a reproduction of Gustave Courbet’s A Burial at Ornans. Both paintings are frieze-like in structure: In the former, the body of an expired or expiring nobleman is conveyed through a turmoil of cattle, dogs, sheep, and milling cavalry; in the latter, a gang of grim-faced locals assembles round an open grave, down at the village cemetery. In both paintings, death is a kind of antimatter, churning the scene.

Am I making it sound random? It’s not random. Some of the galleries are organized around the foundational myths of American culture—work, family, sports—while others are dedicated to a single artist (Maxfield Parrish, for example). It is, however, wildly democratic. Star Wars, as movie geeks know, is a brilliant hodgepodge of influences: Buck Rogers, Kurosawa, The Dam Busters, high culture, trash culture, the lot. At the Lucas Museum, this is part of the character of the collection—everything that tweaked, tickled, or ran its buzzing lightsaber through the imagination of young George Lucas is represented here.

The galleries dedicated to comics and cartoons have a particular energy, pulp art exploding off the walls. Downstairs, meanwhile, on giant screens, are giddyingly depthful high-res photographic re-creations of the Sistine Chapel and, nearby, the Hagia Sophia. The effect is slightly Vegas, that throb of alien vividness, that feeling of signs coming loose from their moorings, the Sphinx gazing blandly across Las Vegas Boulevard—but I love Vegas, and America has taught me to love that feeling. Lucas is also a major collector of that singular populist and freakish master of compacted visual storytelling, Norman Rockwell. I was delighted to be able to stand in front of The Connoisseur—which features a well-dressed older gentleman, seen from the rear (Rockwell loved his rears), his body somewhat torqued with interior tension, standing in front of a large Jackson Pollock–style cosmic splatter. Doing so, I participated, as it were, in its sight gag: a man looking at a painting of a man looking at a painting. Very Rockwellian.

The amplitude of all of this is not for everybody. Writing in the Los Angeles Times in 2017, after it had been announced that the museum was coming to L.A., the critic Christopher Knight protested that narrative art was a “made-up category.” He scorned the definition then on the museum’s website—“Narrative art is visual art that tells a story”—as a “perfect tautology.” Linguistically, he was quite correct, but then again, I’m not sure how you could fail to have a good time at the Lucas Museum, splashing through the gorgeous spaces, bouncing from Diego Rivera to Frank Frazetta. More than that, the conceptual bagginess and ambition and all-gatheringness of the collection is its own statement, as American as it gets. Consciousness is so squeezed right now (close your eyes for two seconds and you’ll feel it) and thieves work the levers of the world, but you leave this museum with a sensation that rumbles in the body for hours—a sensation of art as the most illustrious kind of counterprogramming, art as the vehicle for the real story, which is imagination and connection, which is life.

“The effect of the successful adventure of the hero is the unlocking and release again of the flow of life into the body of the world,” Campbell wrote. Is this what he’s done, 82-year-old Lucas? Streamed the Force right into Exposition Park? Dinged by his Rockwells, donged by his replica Michelangelo, I’m going to say yes. It’s been 21 years since Revenge of the Sith, but this is tremendous storytelling—a killer final act. The hero kneels and opens his hands, and look what comes out: a great and crazy museum, flexing its fins, firing its lasers, swimming like an amphibian through time.

entries.title: What Trump Doesn’t Understand About Xi
entries.summary: The Chinese leader cares very little about personal rapport.
entries.content:
The Chinese leader cares very little about personal rapport.

President Trump will host Xi Jinping for a state visit on September 24, once again putting his claimed bonhomie with the Chinese leader at the center of the relations between the two superpowers. But Trump’s insistence on the importance of this personal rapport shows just how little he understands his adversary.

I have been studying Xi ever since he became China’s heir apparent, and I became an analyst at the CIA in the waning days of the George W. Bush administration. I spent years deciphering Xi for U.S. presidents as the intelligence community’s top expert on Xi. And I spent two years as the director for China at the National Security Council, where I staffed all of President Biden’s interactions with Xi and coordinated diplomacy with China across the U.S. government.

For a decade now, Trump has oscillated between courting and skirmishing with Xi. After his first term, Trump called Xi a friend and described him as someone he knew well. His experience with Xi seems to have led him to believe that he has unique, firsthand insights into China’s leader that his staff and advisers lack; in the past year, he has excluded even his close confidants, such as Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, from intensive diplomacy with China, and has acted practically as his own China desk officer.

Trump’s go-to stratagem for gaining leverage with Xi has been to be unpredictable, or at least to try to be. Yet in Trump’s second term, Xi has surprised Trump more often than Trump has surprised him. That is because Xi’s modus operandi, at home and abroad, is that of a jack-in-the-box: He winds up patiently over years, sometimes decades, and then pops at the propitious moment. The result is always startling.

Xi rose to become China’s leader in large part by presenting himself as having the steady hands needed to restart stalled economic reforms without upsetting the comfortable gentlemen’s agreements that kept the Communist Party’s factional rivalries in check. But once Xi secured power, he launched a blistering campaign against the very party elites who had pulled him up.

Xi’s steeliness has caught Trump off guard, just as it did his Chinese colleagues. At the time of Trump’s first term, Xi was accustomed to playing politics as a quiet, intense poker match, in which the Chinese leader read the opposing players and considered his own cards with characteristic subtlety. Trump, meanwhile, approached politics and policy making more like a gambler on a hot streak at one of the casinos he owned. During his first encounter with Trump, at Mar-a-Lago in 2017, Xi learned about U.S. air strikes on Syria over a beautiful piece of chocolate cake. He spent the years in between Trump’s first and second terms winding up to deal with a president whose M.O. he now understood—and preparing to pop up when the moment was right.

That moment came early in Trump’s second term. In April 2025, the U.S. president rolled out his “Liberation Day” tariffs, which included some that amounted to a de facto embargo on China. Xi surprised Trump by being the only world leader to retaliate rather than conciliate. Trump was ultimately forced to fold.

In the run-up to the two leaders’ summit in Seoul last fall, Xi again surprised Trump’s team—this time by unfurling an expansive set of export controls on rare earth elements, which ultimately prompted the U.S. to roll back its own export controls on China. Beijing’s willingness to escalate was a remarkable departure from a previous pattern of downplaying differences ahead of such summits, and it underscored that Xi was more interested in curtailing Washington’s ability to target China than in striking a deal.

Accordingly, the meeting in Seoul, and Trump’s subsequent visit to Beijing in May, produced little beyond relatively minor commercial agreements affecting specific firms and sectors. The Trump administration, undoubtedly disappointed by the lack of any meaningful deal to emerge from these summits, chose to emphasize Trump’s efforts to deepen his rapport with Xi. The president evidently believes this personal relationship will allow him to secure deals that advance American interests.

This expectation has no observable foundation in Xi’s 14-year rule. Even by the standards of authoritarian rulers, such as Russia’s Vladimir Putin, Xi has shown himself to be unsentimental about personal relationships—including those with members of his own inner circle, to say nothing of the leader of China’s principal geopolitical rival. Xi is very different from Putin in this regard. Whereas Putin takes extravagant risks on the international stage but is loath to hold his associates accountable for incompetence, Xi is just the opposite. He is calculating and measured in international politics but pitiless in jettisoning even longtime associates for perceived malfeasance.

In January, Xi dismissed his military’s top officer, General Zhang Youxia. The relationship between Xi and Zhang went back decades, extending not just to their childhoods but all the way back to their fathers, who were comrades in arms in China’s ferocious civil war. Four years ago, Xi deferred Zhang’s retirement, keeping him on board to help manage the world’s largest and second-most-capable military. We do not know what motivated Xi to oust Zhang, but given the history between the two men, the act was as brutal and unexpected as anything in a season finale of Game of Thrones.

Xi’s approach to Washington has been similarly dispassionate. During Trump’s visit to Beijing, the American president lavished praise on Xi, only for the Chinese leader to respond with stoic indifference.

Trump’s desire to parlay personal charisma into deals may be one of his least idiosyncratic qualities. In fact, there is something about the impulse that is quintessentially American. Even—perhaps especially—for a Beltway outsider, ascending the American political ladder requires a tremendous amount of glad-handing and personal magnetism, if not charm. Those who reach its pinnacle often assume that the same qualities will serve them on the international stage. Joe Biden rose through the Senate, which required cordiality and the ability to strike deals with rivals. George W. Bush and Bill Clinton were known for their affability. Overbearing friendliness might even be described as our national affect.

By contrast, Xi grew up in a system that punished openness and personal dynamism. His father’s boss and mentor, the reformer Hu Yaobang, whose death in 1989 sparked the protests in Tiananmen Square, was known for his outspokenness, which played a crucial role in his political demise. Hu’s ouster extinguished freewheeling politicking from the ranks of China’s leadership ever after.

Going into his next encounter with Xi, Trump seems to genuinely believe that he has the upper hand. Yet an unsettling split screen has accompanied every summit of his second term. In Seoul, Xi walked into the meeting having just outlined the five-year plan for China’s development through 2030. By contrast, Trump was in the midst of the longest government shutdown in U.S. history. In May, Xi hosted Trump for a meeting that Trump had earlier postponed because of the war in Iran, which was going badly. Xi now plans to follow his state visit to Washington with a major party meeting to lay the groundwork for his fourth five-year term, which will start next year. Trump, meanwhile, will be at best a lame-duck president within weeks of the summit—or worse, if the Democrats are able to take back the House or the Senate.

The contrast evident at these meetings with Trump has surely reinforced Xi’s view of the United States as a declining but dangerous power, and of China as an ascendant one. Xi believes that time is on his side, so he does not need a deal. He’s happy to perpetuate an uneasy stalemate through a pantomime of rapport with Trump. In the meantime, Xi is winding up for the fifth U.S presidential administration of his tenure, whatever it may bring.

entries.title: The Biggest Obstacle to Universal Child Care: Babies
entries.summary: Infant care is incredibly expensive to provide. But one solution could reduce the burden on both states and parents.
entries.content:
Infant care is incredibly expensive to provide. But one solution could reduce the burden on both states and parents.

Last year seemed like a pretty big one for breakthroughs in child care. In New York City, Zohran Mamdani’s promise of publicly funded care for young kids helped him win the keys to Gracie Mansion. Officials in Connecticut created an endowment to make care more affordable in that state. And New Mexico became the first state to commit to free child care for all of its residents. But as policy makers have begun hammering out the details of these ambitions, they’ve hit against a stubborn and formidable obstacle: babies.

Any child-care provider will tell you that “affordable infant care” is an oxymoron. Because babies need a ton of individual attention, they are the most demanding group to care for in formal settings. Most states require babies to be looked after by more workers and in smaller groups than those mandated for older kids; a day care’s infant room will typically have one caretaker for every three to four babies, whereas a pre-K teacher might look after more than twice that number of children. Many states and cities also have costly space prerequisites for infant care. In New York City, for instance, a day care’s infant room must have sprinklers installed and be on the ground floor to allow for easy evacuation. All of this drives up the cost of care; one estimate placed the monthly cost of “high-quality” infant care at more than $2,400, a price that only well-off families can afford.

At many child-care centers, the tuition paid for older children subsidizes the babies. “Infants are cute little loss leaders,” Josh McCabe, the director of social policy at the moderate-leaning Niskanen Center think tank, told me. Some programs—because they subsist on razor-thin margins and can be prone to worker shortages—stay clear of babies altogether. (Consider 2-K, Mamdani’s new child-care program for the general public; as the name implies, it does not cover children under 2, even though families with very young children need affordable care as much as anyone else.) This can make infant care a rarity in the places that need it most, including low-income neighborhoods, where the cost of baby care far outpaces what many parents can pay, and rural areas, where day cares serving children of any age are few and far between.

States and cities are thus likely to “hit a wall” when trying to ramp up infant care, Brian Dew, an economic researcher who recently wrote a report comparing the U.S. and Nordic child-care systems, told me. Yet one fair, cost-effective solution could provide relief both to parents and to governments seeking to provide high-quality care: Pay families to keep babies home.

That idea might at first sound odd. But almost every country with universal child care provides a version of this benefit, which allows parents to spend more time with their young children or pay, say, grandparents or neighbors to do it. In the United States, this sort of allowance could help reduce the burden on governments trying to implement universal care and give parents with babies an option that many say they want. It’s also a proposal with growing appeal among a politically diverse set of policy makers.

Traditionally, incentives to keep more young kids (and, by extension, their mothers) home have been associated with conservative politicians. Progressives have focused on increasing access to child care so that parents can work. More broadly, the notion of paying to keep some children home, specifically as part of an effort to offer universal child care, has been “an under-explored area of family policy,” Pete Nabozny, the director of policy at the advocacy organization the Children’s Agenda, told me. But in recent years, the idea has been catching on.

In 2024, Democratic Representative Ro Khanna of California proposed a child-care plan that would not only reduce the cost of formal care but also compensate caregiving relatives and provide a stipend for stay-at-home parents opting out of formal care. In July, Project 2029, the progressive effort to create a policy agenda for a future Democratic administration, released a proposal to allow parents to choose between free child care or a cash benefit of $1,000 a month “to provide care at home or help pay someone they choose to provide care.” And in a forthcoming report, the Niskanen Center suggests reviving a largely defunct effort from the 1990s and early 2000s, when Montana and Minnesota tested programs offering low-income parents the chance to stay home with their babies while receiving a stipend of about the amount that would have gone toward formal care.

Such plans should not be confused with the Trump administration’s recent proposal to redirect dollars from a finite pot of child-care funds to married stay-at-home parents—a move that is almost certain to give fewer, not more, families help in paying for child care. As Jessica Grose noted in The New York Times, it is especially likely to penalize single mothers. And it seems designed to coax married mothers out of the workforce.

Meanwhile, state and city officials who earnestly want to offer more families child care continue to seek solutions and shortcuts to create more spaces for babies. Last year, Vermont increased the reimbursement rates paid to providers for infants and toddlers as part of a bid to expand care for infants; this does appear to have helped generate additional slots for very young children, though still not enough to meet families’ needs. This year, New Mexico reduced zoning barriers to make it easier for licensed child-care programs to operate in private homes, where most infants are cared for.

Then there is Mamdani’s plan for New York City—which so far mostly sidesteps the issue of infant care. His administration has said that it does not plan to extend universal care to infants during the current term, which some policy experts warn is shortsighted. Research on the national expansion of universal pre-K programs found that when public child-care programs for older kids move into a neighborhood, providers serving younger children tend to shift to serving the older, more profitable kids, intensifying care shortages for the youngest. Nabozny said that researchers closely watching the rollout in New York are concerned that Mamdani’s plan may replicate this trend: that it will make infant care even scarcer and, where it is available, more expensive.

This is where offering parents a paid option to care for their babies at home—while also providing more infant care at centers and home-based day cares—starts to make sense. Such an incentive would help take the pressure off formal child-care systems to create more infant-care slots than may be possible. Reducing the number of infants in care outside the home would also make it easier to keep ratios lower for babies in traditional programs, giving kids a better shot at receiving the close attention they need. It would put money in the pockets of families who have recently welcomed a baby—an economically precarious time of transition, when expenses spike and working outside the home can be unfeasible for some mothers. And it would lower costs for states, cities, and counties looking to offer universal care programs, increasing their odds of success.

But arguably the most crucial benefit is that the paid option would give parents something they say they desire, Alyson Silkowski, a senior policy adviser at New America and a co-author of the Project 2029 proposal, told me. Silkowski co-wrote a recent New America report based on a nationally representative survey that oversampled low-income parents; it found that, given the choice, more than a third of parents with children younger than 12 months said they would like to care for their babies themselves throughout the day—a preference that declines once a child turns 1. More than half of those parents want their baby to be looked after by at least one of the child’s parents, Silkowski later wrote to me. Only 9 percent preferred formal care. “There is this higher level of discomfort,” Silkowski said, “in not being with your youngest child during those first 12 months.”

Most countries with universal child care make it easier for parents to stay home with their babies by using some combination of generous paid-parental-leave programs and child- and home-care allowances. In the Nordic system, public child care typically does not start until age 1, when paid leave tapers off. Parents in Finland can opt for a home-care allowance to continue caring for their children until they are 3, and almost all families take this option for at least a few months; many say that 1 year of age is too early for a child to enter formal care.

In the United States, by contrast, few parents have access to paid family leave to care for a newborn, and many can’t afford unpaid leave, prompting a lot of parents to either leave the workforce or return before their family feels ready. But some precedents do exist for paying low-income parents and their relatives to care for children in lieu of enrolling in subsidized care. New York is one of several states with a popular “friend, family, and neighbor” program that lets families who qualify for subsidies hire someone they know for care. And there was the pilot program in Montana and Minnesota during that earlier welfare-reform era.

McCabe, of the Niskanen Center, told me that although both Democrats and Republicans have proposed similar programs in the years since, those plans never took off—partly because they didn’t fit neatly into the policy buckets of welfare, paid leave, or child care, which prompted some advocates to fear that such programs would divert funds and attention from their core causes. In addition, some critics have worried that paying parents to keep babies at home could prevent mothers who want to return to work from doing so. (Research in other wealthy countries suggests that policies such as paid parental leave actually boost women’s workforce participation, though women with children under age 3 still tend to work less than full-time.)

To Nabozny, the idea that a child-care plan should come equipped with a stipend option for the youngest children is a “no-brainer.” “It’s kind of crazy to say the government will pay some other person $25,000, $30,000, whatever the cost of infant care is for a parent to go to work, but we won’t pay that parent a dollar to provide it themselves,” he said, especially “when that is often the family’s preference.” In recent years, a growing number of advocates and policy makers have argued that care work ought to be treated as an essential piece of American infrastructure. The secret to strengthening the country’s formal child-care infrastructure—counterintuitive as this may sound—may be to pay some parents not to use it.

entries.title: MAGA Is Making the World Safe for Corruption
entries.summary: Far-right ideologues have transformed American foreign policy into a tool of private gain and antidemocratic reaction.
entries.content:
Far-right ideologues have transformed American foreign policy into a tool of private gain and antidemocratic reaction.

This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.

In the summer of 2025, the government of Brazil suddenly found itself in a deep crisis. The Trump administration had unexpectedly imposed 50 percent tariffs on the country’s products, threatening everyone from coffee planters to shoe manufacturers. At the same time, the United States canceled the visas of eight Brazilian supreme-court justices and placed unprecedented financial and travel sanctions on a powerful justice and his family.

Many things about this crisis were novel. For the first time anyone could remember, an American administration had used tariffs not for economic reasons but as a tool to influence the internal politics of a friendly democracy. President Trump was publicly fulminating against what he called the “WITCH HUNT” against Jair Bolsonaro, the former president of Brazil, who was then on trial for plotting to carry out a coup after losing an election in 2022. Some of Bolsonaro’s followers had stormed Brazil’s Parliament and other federal buildings, likely inspired by the actions of Trump supporters on January 6, 2021. Steve Bannon, who called the Brazilian insurrectionists “freedom fighters,” was one of many MAGA boosters who cheered them on. When combined with local grievances, the language of American election denial was right at home in Brazil.

The U.S. has used financial sanctions and visa bans in the past—but only to punish dictators, criminals, and people accused of grand-scale international corruption or brutal atrocities. Brazilian Justice Alexandre de Moraes had never been credibly accused of any of this. But by the Trump administration’s reckoning, he had two strikes against him: First, de Moraes’s court was trying Bolsonaro; second, he had provoked the ire of Elon Musk, Trump’s largest election donor. De Moraes “needs to leave,” Musk said, comparing him to Voldemort, after de Moraes threatened to fine X and ordered it to block accounts accused of spreading disinformation.

The crisis was novel in other ways too. In normal times, the Brazilian government is reasonably well connected in Washington, regardless of who runs either country. The tenth-largest economy in the world, Brazil cooperates extensively with U.S. law enforcement and regional organizations. Yet at this crucial moment, with billions of dollars in the balance and Brazil’s sovereign democracy under attack, Brazilian officials suddenly found that nobody in the Trump administration would speak to the formal representatives of their left-leaning president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Brazil’s ambassador to Washington found herself isolated. The foreign minister, a diplomat who had known U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio for decades, could not get through to anyone. A junior official told me that even his graduate-school classmate at the U.S. Treasury would not answer his calls.

The Brazilian finance minister at the time, Fernando Haddad, finally managed to schedule a call with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. But two days before the meeting was to take place, the Treasury Department canceled it—and then Bessent used the same time slot to meet with Eduardo Bolsonaro, the former president’s son. The younger Bolsonaro—who lives in Texas, has befriended Donald Trump Jr., and attends Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) meetings—was flaunting his connections in Washington, which were manifestly better than those of Lula’s administration.

That put the Brazilians in a strange position. “All the official channels that we have, they just suddenly went out of touch,” the junior official told me. “And what happened is that myriad informal actors just started knocking at our doors. And that was interesting.”

Some of these visitors were types not previously known in Washington: lobbyists advertising their relationships not with government officials but with the people who hang around Mar-a-Lago, or with MAGA influencers whose X accounts can attract the president’s attention. Others were business operators offering government favors while seeking to make deals for themselves: An investor who claimed to own a vacation home near Bessent’s offered to arrange a meeting with the Treasury secretary in exchange for access to crucial minerals for himself. The Brazilians declined that offer.

A truce was finally arranged, multiple people told me, with the help of Joesley Batista, a billionaire whose meatpacking company does business in both the U.S. and Brazil, and whose American subsidiary had donated $5 million to Trump’s inauguration (more than the contributions of Amazon, Meta, and Google combined). Batista had no official government role, but his money may have given him the clout to influence Trump’s meetings with Lula at the 2025 United Nations General Assembly, in New York City, and at a summit in Kuala Lumpur, where the two elderly populists, each with grievances against their respective establishments, hit it off. The tariffs were reduced.

The détente was temporary. When I visited São Paulo and Brasília this past spring, the State Department had just appointed a new senior adviser on Brazil policy. Before working for the administration, Darren Beattie founded Revolver News, a website that promoted the “Fedsurrection” conspiracy—the belief that federal agents were behind the riots on January 6, an obsession that would naturally appeal to Brazil’s election deniers and displease the elected president. When Beattie asked to visit Brazil for a minerals conference, the Brazilian government refused to grant him a visa, in part because it suspected that his true purpose was to visit Jair Bolsonaro, then in prison.

Among the journalists, analysts, and officials I met in Brazil, the main topic of conversation was not whether the U.S. would intervene in the country’s elections this fall but how. Flávio Bolsonaro, another of the ex-president’s sons, is running for president, and the Trump administration seems to be looking for ways to help. In June, when a Brazilian court handed Flávio’s brother Eduardo a prison sentence for seeking to get the U.S. to intervene in his father’s trial, Trump’s State Department denounced the conviction as “lawfare.” In July, the administration planned to send two envoys to Brazil to meet with election deniers and “investigate” the Brazilian electoral system; their visa requests were also turned down. A Brazilian public-policy professor told me he wouldn’t be surprised if American social-media platforms quietly began to help Bolsonaro. These tech companies have already shown that they will “flip ideology” to align with changes in the American government. So why not in Brazil?

Slowly, the Brazilians were learning the same lesson as other American allies around the world: The United States of America is no longer the entity they knew. And American power is no longer deployed solely by trained diplomats and reliable officials, working through state channels. Informal envoys, private companies, online grifters, and hardened ideologues both inside and outside the government matter more. Unlike their predecessors, these people do not talk about spreading democracy, and don’t want to build long-term relationships. They don’t care about America’s reputation. They are deploying the tools of American diplomacy and government for their own purposes, to promote their own business interests or their own ideological goals, because, suddenly, they can.

“Revolutions are the locomotives of history,” Karl Marx wrote. He was wrong about many things but not about this: In modern times, every major revolutionary movement has sought to change not just the politics of a single country but the international system itself. Napoleon marched the French Revolution across Europe. Lenin and Trotsky believed that their Bolshevik Revolution would succeed only when the Soviet Union was surrounded by other Communist states. Ayatollah Khomeini and his successors built proxy movements to spread their ideology across the Middle East.
