Orbán, before losing his election, appeared with Carlson and invited him to a public event in Hungary, to demonstrate to Hungarians that he had American support.

Rallies for revolutionary allies. Meetings of CPAC, once a mainstream forum for U.S. conservatives, have now become a kind of traveling road show that appears wherever sponsors can pay, offering visibility and quasi-official American endorsements to the local far right. A rotating team of international guests shows up: Bolsonaro, Simion, Bukele, Orbán, Milei, and Weidel, as well as Geert Wilders of the Dutch far right and Santiago Abascal of the Spanish far right. They join Americans such as Kristi Noem, Senator Ted Cruz, and Trump’s consigliere Richard Grenell.

Repurposing humanitarian agencies to benefit revolutionary allies. Discarding decades of human-rights standards and refugee law, the Trump administration removed refugee-processing officials from postings around the world and sent them to South Africa, where they are helping allegedly repressed Afrikaners (who do not by any international standard qualify as refugees). The officials did their job: From October 2025 through June 2026, the U.S. accepted 7,727 “refugees” from South Africa—and three from the rest of the world. An additional 10,000 white South Africans are on track to be accepted soon. A government estimate puts the cost of processing them at $100 million.

Following the destruction of USAID, Food for Peace—a program that has fed more than 4 billion people over 70 years—was moved to the Department of Agriculture, where its primary purpose will be not fighting hunger around the world but subsidizing U.S. farmers. This year, it will distribute food to countries that, for obscure reasons, don’t include those on the edge of famine, notably Sudan, South Sudan, and Somalia—but will include El Salvador, whose leader is a friend of the revolution.

Congressional networking with revolutionary allies. In March, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson headlined an Alliance of Sovereign Nations conference, hosted by Turning Point Action, bringing members of Congress and the global far right together beneath the banner of the organization created by the late Charlie Kirk. Among the attendees were Markus Frohnmaier, an AfD leader with unusually close ties to Russia; leaders from Georgia and Azerbaijan, repressive states with close ties to Russia; and Anna Paulina Luna, the conference organizer, a Florida congresswoman with close ties to Russia. George Simion was also there, having appeared earlier in the year as a guest at a party at the Kennedy Center, where he cut a slice from a red-white-and-blue cake shaped like Greenland.

Ending democracy promotion. All of the U.S. government institutions created over decades to promote democratic ideas and practices have now been weakened, dismantled, or rewired to promote the revolution. USAID is gone; foreign broadcasters such as Voice of America and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty have barely survived; the State Department’s annual Country Reports on Human Rights Practices, once considered a nonpartisan source of information on human rights, now suggests that Germany is more oppressive than El Salvador. Slowly, the money the U.S. spends on educational and cultural programs, scholarships, and exchange-student programs—a cornerstone of U.S. foreign policy and soft power since the early 1960s—is being repurposed. One example: 11 out of 12 members of the Fulbright exchange-student program’s board resigned last year after the State Department canceled nearly 200 Fulbright scholarships for American academics approved by the board and put other awards under review. One of the former board members told PBS that the board feared that the department was trying to block politically incorrect projects. This marked—“for the first time in 80 years,” he said—the “interjection of politics into the selection process,” a “gross distortion” of the program.

Asked at an event about the Trump administration’s policy toward cultural and academic grants more generally, Sarah Rogers, who runs America’s public diplomacy, explained that “we would choose a winning applicant for most of these grants based on how credibly we thought that person or organization could advance American priorities.” But what are “American priorities” if the American government is run by people who use its instruments not on behalf of its citizens, but on behalf of themselves?

Revolutions inspire other revolutions—and counterrevolutions. America is producing both. Slowly, politics around the world are shifting as leaders copy Trump’s tactics, switch sides to curry favor, develop a sudden interest in crypto—or else try hard to hedge against the predatory American regime.

Although European nationalist parties have historically favored a heavy role for the state—Viktor Orbán’s Hungary was an excellent example—many have now adopted a libertarian message, aligning themselves both with Trump and with American and international companies that seek havens from government regulation. Nigel Farage, the leader of the British far-right Reform party, campaigned for Trump in 2024. Now his income streams look similar to Trump’s. In 2024, he accepted a $6.7 million personal donation from a Thailand-based crypto mogul, Christopher Harborne, allegedly for Farage’s “security.” And George Cottrell, a convicted fraudster, also appears to have funded both Farage and, via donations made by Cottrell’s mother, Reform (even as a Polymarket account in Cottrell’s name was receiving some $9 million in cryptocurrency from unidentified sources). Previously better-known for promoting Brexit, Farage began to lobby hard on crypto issues—for example, he opposed a Bank of England cryptocurrency project that, as it happens, would damage Harborne’s business.

The revolution has also arrived in Poland, where the previously domestic-facing nationalist right has developed links to both the cryptocurrency industry and the Trump administration. A currency exchange called Zondacrypto, now under investigation for allegedly swindling customers, sponsored the CPAC event in Poland where Kristi Noem endorsed Karol Nawrocki and reportedly made contributions to foundations created by right-wing politicians. After Nawrocki won, he vetoed—three times—the centrist Polish government’s attempts to enshrine consumer cryptocurrency protections into Polish law. Echoing the language used in Trump’s Washington, Nawrocki’s justification for vetoing referenced “freedom” and “innovation.” (Disclosure: My husband, Radek Sikorski, is the foreign minister of Poland’s centrist government.)

In Latin America, hard-right politicians, some openly imitating Trump’s language and style, and some with links to crypto or the world of anonymous shell companies, are beginning to gain traction. Bukele, the autocratic leader of El Salvador, anticipated the revolution. He declared bitcoin legal tender in 2021, recruited an array of crypto-evangelists into his administration, and built a parallel diplomatic corps that set up Salvadoran bitcoin “embassies” in Texas and Switzerland. He also constructed a maximum-security prison for alleged gang members, designed with performative cruelty. The Trump administration sent alleged criminals there early in 2025. (Later investigations would find that most had no criminal records.)

Other Latin American leaders are also drawing from the Trump-Bukele playbook. Trump endorsed the new president of Colombia, Abelardo de la Espriella, a businessman who once told Agence France-Presse that “people who have created wealth during their lives should run the country”—a sentiment that sounds familiar—and who wants to build “mega-prisons” too. Hours after his inauguration, the U.S. offered him a $1 billion “security package,” even as his predecessor, taking another page out of the American playbook, was making accusations of a rigged election. Trump also backed José Antonio Kast, the new president of Chile, who ran a campaign calling for tighter border controls and mass deportations. During his first week in office, Kast negotiated a joint statement with the U.S. on mining rare earth minerals that seems intended to benefit private American mining interests.

Outside the democratic world, where kleptocracy has long been the norm, no special changes are necessary to accommodate the new American regime. Pragmatism reigns: If American-government decisions are now for sale, then many will eagerly buy them. The Qataris did not give Trump a $400 million jumbo jet merely out of friendship. The Saudi public-investment fund did not commit $2 billion to Jared Kushner’s private-equity fund simply as a gesture of goodwill. And Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama did not offer Kushner and Ivanka Trump a piece of the country’s environmentally protected coastline to build a luxury resort because he admires their design sense.

Sometimes, these kinds of contributions appear aimed at achieving very specific results. Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the Emirati royal family, purchased a 49 percent stake in World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s cryptocurrency venture, for $500 million. A few months later, the Trump administration agreed to let the UAE buy high-tech chips whose export the Biden administration had restricted.

Most governments in the old democratic world cannot compete in this race. Europeans, Canadians, Australians, and others can’t pay off the American president by investing in his children’s companies, because that would be illegal. Nor are they finding it easy to adjust to the new world of quasi-official, quasi-private diplomacy.

Instead they are beginning to look elsewhere for contacts, for technology, for trade. No one previously imagined that Canada would find it necessary to sign a defense pact with the EU, let alone to conduct defense-tech negotiations with Australia; it has now done both. The EU has just arranged a free-trade agreement with India, something that few people were interested in completing a few years ago, and another with Australia. In the first half of 2026, no fewer than 26 world leaders visited China, including the British, Spanish, German, and Canadian prime ministers. The French government is slowly removing Windows, Microsoft Teams, and Zoom from its computers, replacing them with open-source software or French-made alternatives. Some German regional governments, as well as the Danish and Dutch governments, are on a similar mission, as are some European banks and universities. These changes are meant to be permanent. After all, even if a Democrat wins the White House in 2028, the companies empowered by federal money and the ideologues who have taken over institutions will continue to influence Congress and voters. Now that Trump has shown that it can be done, future presidents might also benefit from kleptocratic practices. “We cannot leave the security of Europe in the hands of voters in Wisconsin every four years,” France’s Europe minister has said.

These shifts have been mocked and attacked by some, including the Pentagon’s Elbridge Colby, who has argued that American allies can’t replace the U.S. That may be true, in the short term. But if Colby or anyone else believes that America’s old friends will not stop looking for other options, then he has misunderstood the depth and profundity of the shift in perceptions of America, not just in a few capital cities but in the heads and hearts of people around the globe.

A trivial but revealing incident from this summer hints at the extent of the change. Remember Trump’s phone call to Gianni Infantino, the president of FIFA, the body that runs the World Cup? Folarin Balogun, America’s star striker, had been given a red card, making him ineligible for the team’s next game, against Belgium. Trump asked Infantino to review the ban. FIFA lifted it. “I’m a person that loves sports and was a good athlete,” Trump told reporters, “and I understand sports really well. Really well.” But Trump did not understand sports, or sports fans. The outrage was immediate, visceral, and international, not because of anything the U.S. team had done but because the U.S. president had assumed he was allowed to break the rules, and because so many Americans seemed to approve.

Few may care about the ins and outs of Brazilian politics or understand the business dealings of World Liberty Financial. But many can recognize cheating. The head of the Norwegian football association filed an ethics complaint because “when you bend a rule like this, you’re on a slippery slope that will put the whole game at risk.” The British journalist Hugo Rifkind wrote that he was “startled and troubled to find myself heavily invested in Belgium winning a football game.” I heard former Italian Prime Minister Enrico Letta tell a large European audience that “Italians, French, and, yes, even the Dutch” had all rooted for Belgium too. I spent a couple of hours looking at commentary; hundreds of thousands, maybe even millions, of fans from all over the world left angry comments on X, YouTube, Facebook. The story resonated, not because this one World Cup match mattered, but because the presumptuous disdain that America showed for everyone else was so familiar.

Maybe it resonated with the team too. When the U.S. lost to Belgium—and lost badly—some wondered if Trump’s move had unsettled the players. They surely knew that the world was rooting against them, and seemed to have lost belief in themselves as a result. Other Americans may soon come to the same conclusion. For decades, we have told ourselves that our country represents democracy, freedom, and free trade. We believed we had allies, like-minded nations that shared these values. We thought we opposed dictators and kleptocrats, the leaders who steal from their own people. What happens when we realize that we no longer do?

This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “Empire of Grift.”

Today The Atlantic is launching The Permanent Questions, a new video podcast hosted by staff writer David Brooks about the fundamental questions of human life that every generation—and every individual—must attempt to answer. In new episodes publishing every Sunday, David will engage thinkers, writers, and artists in conversations about what makes us human, what gives life meaning, and how we can build richer relationships and a more just society.



For the first episode, available today, David is joined by Meghan Sullivan, the Wilsey Family College Professor of Philosophy at the University of Notre Dame, to consider what it means to live a good life. In an introduction to the show, David says: “There are a lot of shows about politics and business and health and tech, but there aren’t enough about the really big questions of life.”



The podcast builds on David’s decades of writing about political, cultural, moral, and social issues. David joined The Atlantic’s staff after many years as a contributing writer, and has recently written about the crucial lessons for the Democratic Party; “The People Who Will Thrive in the AI Age,” about why people’s relationship to mental effort will differentiate them; how “History Is Running Backwards” and why reactionaries are taking over the world; and “Something Big Is Happening on Campus,” on how plenty is going wrong in American higher education, but a lot is also going right.



The launch of The Permanent Questions is part of a continued surge of audio and video at The Atlantic, which has doubled its number of weekly shows, podcast staff, and audio revenue in the past year. Since 2025, The Atlantic has launched the video podcasts The David Frum Show and Galaxy Brain with Charlie Warzel, and this past summer expanded its flagship show, Radio Atlantic—co-hosted by Hanna Rosin and Adam Harris, with a weekly Monday video episode hosted by Adam.



The podcast is produced by The Atlantic and made possible by support from Yale University, where David is also a presidential senior fellow at Yale Jackson School of Global Affairs. Episodes of The Permanent Questions will be released each Sunday. Viewers can subscribe to watch on The Atlantic’s YouTube channel or wherever they get their podcasts. Please reach out with any questions or requests.

entries.title: What Is the Good Life?
entries.summary: The philosophy professor Meghan Sullivan doesn’t just want to teach her students about virtue; she wants to make them better human beings.
entries.content:
The philosophy professor Meghan Sullivan doesn’t just want to teach her students about virtue; she wants to make them better human beings.

Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube

In the debut episode of The Permanent Questions With David Brooks, David speaks with the philosopher Meghan Sullivan about perhaps the most important question of them all: How should we live our lives? Sullivan is a co-author of The Good Life Method, based on a popular course she teaches at Notre Dame. Leading a good life, she argues, means not just maximizing our positive impact in the world, but cultivating virtue within our own souls. Along the way, David and Sullivan discuss Iris Murdoch, finding bliss at CVS, and exercising our philosophical muscles before life slaps us in the face.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

David Brooks: Hi, I’m David Brooks. If you are listening to or watching this, you’ve stumbled across the first episode of a new podcast called The Permanent Questions.

The idea of the podcast is that there are a lot of shows about politics and business and health and tech, but there aren’t enough about the really big questions of life. How do you find your purpose? How do you confront death? How do you save a relationship that’s going through a rough patch? How do you build a just society?

Now, you may be asking yourself, “How the hell did a political pundit get into these deep waters?”

When I was 18, an incredibly lucky thing happened to me: The admissions officers at Columbia University, Wesleyan, and Brown decided I should go to the University of Chicago. I didn’t know anything about Chicago. I’d never visited. I never knew anybody who went there, but it was the only school I got into.

It turned out to be the perfect school for me. My favorite joke about Chicago: It’s a Baptist school where atheist professors teach Jewish students Saint Thomas Aquinas. And I fit right in.

There’s a saying, “If you catch fire with enthusiasm, people will come for miles to watch you burn.” My professors had caught fire with enthusiasm.

Those teachers were filled with a certain conviction. The conviction was, if you read important books, had important conversations, and addressed big questions, you would have the keys to the kingdom.

They gave us new things to love: new ideas, new heroes, new activities, new subjects. They tried to teach us how to see, not only to see with your preconceptions and the things you think you see, but to see with the clarity of a Tolstoy, the moral depth of George Eliot, the empathetic outrage of James Baldwin.

Mostly, they introduced us to the Great Conversation. The Great Conversation is a tradition of debate that goes back for thousands of years. It’s a collective attempt to find a workable balance between the inevitable tensions of life—the tension between autonomy and belonging, between freedom and order, between diversity and cohesion, safety and exploration, tenderness and strength, intellect and passion. The Great Conversation never ends, because there is no permanent solution to these tensions, just a temporary resting spot that works in this or that circumstance.

I never wanted to leave the Great Conversation, and I never have. I went off and became a journalist and a political pundit, and that was a worthwhile thing to do, and I still do it. A lot of the big questions in life are political questions. Who should lead us? What does a just society even look like? But none of my six books are about politics. They’re about the kind of questions my teachers asked me back in Chicago: How do you educate your emotions? How do you survive a setback?

As my career has gone on, I came to the conclusion that we as a society are over-politicized and under-moralized. That is to say, we pay attention to every little political scandal, but many people have been given no instruction on the basic questions of how to live, of how they should find their calling, what they should really want.

And over the last 15 years or so, this sensation has taken a deeper urgency. Like a lot of countries, America seems to be going through some sort of spiritual, relational, and social, and maybe moral crisis. You know all the stats: rising loneliness, rising despair, rising distrust, rising polarization.

We’re living through a period of great technological advance, but we’re losing our humanistic core. Because of technological improvements and social deterioration, our lives are objectively better, but subjectively worse. The elements of civilization that lift the spirit and nurture the affections are playing a smaller and smaller role in our national life. Religion, literature, art, theology, history, philosophy, friendship, even conversation.

In previous periods of technological advance, there was a humanistic counterreaction. Humanists said, “Okay, bring us your science. Bring us your machines. Bring us your efficiency. Bring us your technology. That’s fine. But don’t turn us into machines ourselves.” And the humanists made an aggressive counter-push to say, “We will preserve our humanistic core. We will preserve what is essentially human. ”

This podcast is an attempt to be a small part of that kind of humanistic reaction.

We asked Meghan Sullivan to be the first guest on the show because she’s the kind of great teacher I’m talking about. Meghan teaches one of the most beloved courses at Notre Dame University, which is called “God and the Good Life.” She’s won Notre Dame’s Joyce Award for Excellence in Teaching, and as you’ll see, she’s got a dynamic personality. She co-authored a book based on the course, called The Good Life Method: Reasoning Through the Big Questions of Happiness, Faith, and Meaning.

Meghan doesn’t just do education, providing students with facts they can regurgitate on a test. Meghan does formation. She helps students become better versions of themselves. And so it’s a great pleasure to welcome Meghan Sullivan to this table.

Brooks: Welcome, Meghan Sullivan. You are the first guest on The Permanent Questions. You are the founding figure of our podcast. So thank you for being here.

Meghan Sullivan: Heavy is the crown. This is a tremendous responsibility, David.

Brooks: I know. All future guests will be measured by your exemplary example.

Sullivan: Exactly. I’m hopefully gonna create a large ceiling for this podcast.

Brooks: So, you grew up in North Carolina, and I assume you had a moderately normal childhood. And then you became a philosopher. So how the hell did that happen?

Sullivan: I did not grow up in an academic family. My mom was a receptionist in a dental office, and my dad worked a bunch of different jobs, but for most of high school he worked at this company called Replacements. They basically replaced, like, broken plates. My dad was in the plate-replacement business. My mom was in the dental-billing business. So that was not particularly academic background, but very, very loving. And if you would’ve told me when I was a high-school student that I would end up a philosophy professor, I would have asked you to throw me off a bridge.

Most of my students have never met a professional philosopher before they take my class. But in high school, actually, one of my best friends, her dad was a philosophy professor at our local university, and we were very, very judgy, snotty teenage girls, and we devoted probably two years of high school to thinking, “We cannot understand this guy’s job.”

So in high school, I had a well-considered, extremely negative opinion of the profession of philosophy that was based on nothing but vibes about my friend’s dad’s books.

I got a scholarship and went to the University of Virginia, so this big public school where, as a freshman, you’re just sort of fed into the meat grinder. You just get whatever classes are left over after all of the big kids register for their classes. And my academic adviser was talking to me, and I was so stressed because I couldn’t get any of the pre-law classes that I desperately wanted, or econ classes. And he’s like, “I think that you would really love this ethics class called ‘Issues of Life and Death’ in the philosophy department. It’s really debate-y, and I just think given your background, you’re gonna have a blast in there. ”

So I was like, “Okay, fine. Philosophy. ” And I enrolled in that class, and I was hooked by the second week. The exact moment—I remember this really vividly—I was sitting in Alderman Library, in the library at UVA, and we’d just gotten our first assignment for all of our classes, our first writing assignment, and I was writing all these boring book reports for my other classes.

In “Issues of Life and Death,” the question we were assigned is: “Should you end your life?” And I remember talking to the TA being like, “Do you want me to write about what, you know, David Hume says about suicide?” And he’s like, “Absolutely not. I want the strongest possible argument about whether you should continue living.”

And I was like, “Are you allowed to ask me that? Like, is that allowed?” And he’s like, “Not only is it allowed, but there are better and worse answers, and if you don’t have a really tight, really well-argued position, you’re gonna get a bad grade in this class.” And I just remember sitting in the library, the kind of blinking cursor on Microsoft Word staring at me, thinking, Ah, we’re firing live ammunition here. Like, this is real. And that just totally got me hooked.

Brooks: Now, a lot of philosophers write abstruse academic articles with a lot of notations and numbers and diagrams. You actually teach this class, and you’ve written this book, on how to live. Why’d you become that kind of philosopher?

Sullivan: I had an epiphany my third year at Notre Dame. I was getting ready to go up for tenure, and I’d been teaching our big intro philosophy class. And when you go through the tenure process, at first, you’re only focused on keeping your job, and then you start to hit a point where you imagine a future where you’re just a professor and you’re not worried about getting fired all the time. And I was in that kind of mindset of thinking, What do I wanna do with the rest of my career after I hopefully survive this tenure vote?

And I felt very, very strongly that I wanted to focus the next chapter on my teaching. That’s what really I loved about my job. And I’d been teaching Aristotle. And we inflict Aristotle on every single freshman at the University of Notre Dame. And Aristotle has this line in the second chapter of his book about the good life that I’ve always loved, and I always assign students to write essays about.

He says, “We conduct this examination not so that we can know what virtue is, but so that we might be good.” We do all this not so we can know what dead people said about virtue and philosophy, but so that we can become happier people. Otherwise, there’s no benefit of it, he says. This whole enterprise is pointless if it doesn’t find some way to make us better.

Brooks: Now, you’re in the business of helping people become, as you said, happy and good. And this podcast is in the same business. I’m joining your team.

Sullivan: Yeah, all right.

Brooks: And so, as we enter this conversation, I thought I’d raise some objections to the life we have chosen.

Sullivan: Bring it. Objections are the love language of philosophy.

Brooks: So the first one is what’s—why is this necessary? I get up in the morning; I have my Frappuccino; I surf my media feed; I go to work, which is good, I like my work; I go home; I watch Netflix. Why should I read a bunch of complicated books and have hard conversations?

Sullivan: So one assumption I think we should challenge is that there are some people who do philosophy, a small number of people, like my friend’s dad, and then everybody else doesn’t do philosophy.

That’s like saying there are some people who exercise, and everybody else doesn’t exercise. I get why you’d make that assumption if you think that exercise or philosophy is this really, really narrow prescribed activity. But that’s just not true.

My doctor would be the first person to tell you, you use your body every single day. It’s just some people exercise well and train, and other people are potatoes (Laughs.) like me. Which is why my doctor brings this up all the time.

It’s the same with philosophy. If we think about philosophy in the ancient tradition, like Socrates’s tradition, philosophy is caring for your soul. And everybody has to do this. It’s just a question about whether or not you’re gonna do it well or you’re gonna do it in a really immature way. You could do better or worse at reasoning through these soul questions that are—they’re gonna slap you in the face. If you don’t use your philosophical muscle, then you’re gonna find it pretty atrophied at these junctures in life when you really need it.

Brooks: Let me know what you think of my answer. My answer would be: We live in a dangerous world, a spiritually dangerous world. You graduate, and you enter modern America, modern society, and there are a couple temptations.

The first is you’re gonna lead an aesthetic life. Well, I think Kierkegaard came up with this. An aesthetic life is like, you have some happy, pleasant experiences, and you treat all of life as: How can I have more pleasant experiences? And you treat your life sort of as a consumer. And that strikes me as a shallow way to live, and not a sturdy way to live, because you don’t have the substance to survive the hard times.

The second is, and I see this in a lot of my students, you become an insecure overachiever. You don’t know what your purpose is, you don’t know what the foundation of your life is, so you think you can make your life better by building a series of successive stories on top of a foundation made of sand, and eventually that comes crashing down.

And third, Iris Murdoch—who’s this novelist and philosopher—she said the purpose of life is to become more virtuous. Like, that’s the whole deal. And so to me, it’s almost a way to resist the temptations of the world.

Sullivan: I love Iris Murdoch. This is a deep cut probably for a lot of folks. They don’t know that she’s one of the great philosophers of the 20th century. But one of the things I love about Murdoch is, you read her essays—which can be pretty dense; I wouldn’t jump in in the deep end in her philosophical essays—but she always has these examples that strike me as very true to life.

And one of her examples is, she comes out of a faculty meeting, and she realizes she just really despises her colleague, who’s just irritating, and she can’t quite put her finger on what she doesn’t like about this woman, but she just doesn’t like her. And she’s sitting in her office, and she’s stewing, and it’s threatening to ruin her day, and then she realizes, she has this moment of realization that she can reconsider this person. She has free will. She can sit there and just ask herself to look again or imagine this person again, and that she’s not just a victim of her prejudices or situation, but in fact she’s able to work on her inner life just as much as she’s able to work on her career.

And it’s hard, but reading examples like that, I think she practiced what she preached. She really strived.

Brooks: She wrote one book that I could understand, which is called The Sovereignty of Good, I think it was called. And it’s short, and it’s very clear. And the thing I loved about it is that she was a devotee of Simone Weil, the French mystic from World War II era, basically, and Weil once said, “Attention is the ultimate form of generosity.” And Iris Murdoch builds on that. And she says, You think morality is mostly about what you do, but a lot of it is just how you attend to people. And she said, sort of as the story you’d said, You should cast a just and loving attention on people. And I like that, because it’s loving, but it’s also just.

Sullivan: You know who also does this? This is always so surprising, and I point this out to my students: Everybody thinks that the Stoics are these hard, emotionless robots, like the ancient Roman philosophers. But if you read Marcus Aurelius—who was the emperor of Rome and who killed scores of barbarians, right, was, like, a hard-core general—you read his Meditations, and the opening chapter of it is just a long list of all of the specific people he loves and what they have meant to him in his life. Before he gets into how to kill barbarians and be stronger and wake up at 5 a.m. and meditate, he thinks about love, and he pays attention to all of the people that have made him the man that he is.

Brooks: Second challenge: Okay, I wanna become a better person, but that’s the job for religion or family. Why the hell does a teacher think he or she can influence my life? Like, what business is it of hers?

Sullivan: It’s funny, I think the public discourse kind of wants to have it both ways. Sometimes they’re incredibly worried about college corrupting the youth in bad ways, like, giving the youth crazy ideas about politics or the way society works. Or, the other half of the time, they’re really nervous that they send their kid to college and nothing happens, and it wasn’t worth the money. I think this is a shame, because we have one of the most extraordinary higher-education systems in world history in the United States right now.

These universities that we’ve built painstakingly over 300, 350 years, they have always had these dual functions. They are places where you go to learn a trade and where the truth is kind of cultivated and maintained about all manner of subjects, but they’re also places where people go to be formed. And there’s a reason why in the college system from England and the United States, there’s typically a chapel and a refectory—a dining hall—and dormitories, and they have the kind of setup of a medieval monastery, is the idea, that we’re gonna take these folks who are just emerging on adult life and give them a period of focus and discernment before they set out on their odyssey, and that that’s a really tremendous and important gift that we offer to each successive generation that comes after us.

And for those of us who’ve had the benefit of a college education, and there’s only a handful of people in my family that have gone away to college, you see it. Not because we’re, like, morally better. I’m definitely not any morally better than my brother who didn’t go away to college and dropped out of high school. If you respectfully ask somebody to tell you the story of their life, no one has ever asked them, and they’re delighted to do this.

Sullivan: We started teaching this Good Life class 10 years ago, so it’s the 10-year anniversary. And one of the things we have all the students do is write this long confessional essay, basically, their confessions like Augustine, their apology like Socrates, where they share key moments from their life and then debate with themselves about what its significance is in light of the philosophy that we’ve been reading in class.

And this is 40 percent of their grade, this one big confessional essay. And I remember when we were unleashing the course, I got a lot of criticism from well-meaning but mistaken faculty who basically said, “You cannot ask a student to disclose aspects of their life like this. That’s professionally inappropriate. And you can’t grade them on it, you fool. This is not possible. ”

And we don’t grade them based on are they good people or not. We grade them based on their philosophical reasoning. But I have taught thousands of students in the last decade in this class. I have never once had a student complain about going through this exercise.

Sometimes they’ll complain about their final grade, but they never complain about the self-disclosure part. It’s the opposite. I get notes and emails from students, oftentimes from their parents, often like a year after they’ve taken the class, saying, “Hey, I just want you to realize that meant a tremendous amount to me at the time. Nobody had ever listened to me or paid that much attention to me in my life.”

Brooks: I’ve gotta ask, I was curious about this, about the apology. Like, they’re 18, 19, whatever. What do they say?

Sullivan: There are some common themes. They have to pick three of 10 possible topics.

Politics, money, work, moral responsibility, suffering, love, death, God, contemplation, et cetera. I think I got nine out of the 10. They tend to always pick three. They never pick politics. You’d be shocked to learn, they never think that political debate is a very important part of their lives, which is hilarious because we’re constantly pressured now as faculty to teach our students how to have political debates, this is all the rage right now, and I wanna tell them, none of my students actually care that much about this topic. Maybe they should, but they just don’t.

They usually choose work and love. My students are obsessed with work. That part of their essays tends to be very funny, because I will more often than not read these extremely sincere sections of their essays about their experiences with what Karl Marx calls alienation from your “species-being,” which is when you feel like the capitalist conditions you’re forced to operate under separate you from your deep sources of meaning and your essence. And they will say that their experience being the treasurer of the Ultimate Frisbee team has been a constant grind and has caused them to believe that they’re only valuable insofar as what they produce for the Frisbee club, and they’re experiencing burnout because of that.

But they do put a high value on work, and we let them. We indulge that. I give the students about four weeks on work and money in the class to just talk through all their questions, ’cause you can’t try to suppress it.

And then the second big theme is love. And one surprise, or I don’t know if this would be a surprise or not. You would think lovesick college students would write about romantic love and what it means to them. And we do a little bit of readings on that. They never write about romantic love.

The vast majority of my freshmen have actually never had a serious boyfriend or girlfriend by the time I get them. That’s still in the future for them. They write about their parents, and occasionally their siblings. And so I get to read a lot of really beautiful essays about their reflections on what these relationships have meant to them. I think a lot of them are experiencing some homesickness by the time I see them. But that’s very moving. And again, figures like Aristotle that we obsess about in the class, Aristotle gives a whole chapter over to parent-child relationships. These are extremely philosophically rich parts of our lives.

The most profound moment for this actually was in 2020. I was teaching my Good Life class, and I had two young women in the class. This was peak pandemic. Notre Dame went back in person in the fall, so we were all sitting there. We taught that class in the football stadium, and we were all wearing face masks in one of the sky boxes that the donors have in this massive room, and wearing face masks and struggling through the pandemic. And I had two young women in the class, and they’d just worked on the first draft of their apology essay, and they were crossing the street coming back from an event, and were hit by a drunk driver and killed.

And they were international students, and their family had to travel to the United States a few days later for the memorial masses for these two young women, and it was a huge ordeal. And Notre Dame, to their credit, put on this big in-person memorial service for these two women, even though it was really challenging.

And we got to give the parents the first drafts of these essays that these women had written, and they’d both chosen to write about love, unsurprisingly. When people are asked what really matters in their life, that’s one of the key sections. And one in particular had written about how much she loves her brother and what that feels like for her now that they’re separated.

And for us to be able to give—they’d never vocalized these things, or they had maybe in a quick text, like, “LOL, hugging face.” But it had never—their parents had never experienced five single-spaced pages of, “This is what love of you has meant in my life.” And to be able to take that artifact and give that to these grieving family members reminded me: This is the most important thing we could do.

I don’t care, you know, your “Compare and contrast Kant and Marx.” Yeah blah, blah, blah. That’s great. This is a little fragment of these women’s souls that we finally managed to wrap our hands around that we could give back to you when the rest of it is just grievously ripped from your hands.

Brooks: Wow. That’s an incredible story. Very moving.

So we’ve talked about love a lot in this conversation, and so my question to you is: Are you in the wrong business? I think of philosophy as about cognition. And so that would imply that being a good person is about having the right beliefs. You guys work on beliefs. But it doesn’t seem to me that being a good person is really mostly about beliefs. If it was, moral philosophers would be better than the rest of us. And sorry, you guys aren’t. I mean, you’re obviously better than the economists.

Sullivan: Yeah, for sure.

Brooks: But, but they’re not better than—

Sullivan: No, definitely not.

Brooks: But then when you think about, say, the church scandals. The guys who abused those children and then covered up for it, they had sat through a million sermons. They probably had the right beliefs. But we would say there was something poisoned in their soul that they are willing to damage another human being or cover up that damage.

So how do you think about the relationship between what I would call the desires and emotions, and reason? Are you too much in the reason business?

Sullivan: I think you could definitely accuse a lot of philosophers of that. My friend Eric Schwitzgebel did this really interesting study about, a social-psychology study, where he basically looked at whether your typical professional philosopher is more or less moral in everyday decision making than the kinda standard human. And you’ll be shocked, stunned to learn that your typical philosopher is a little bit less honest in ordinary situations, a little bit less moral than maybe their baseline American.

But this should not come as a surprise to those of us who study the tradition of philosophy. Aristotle, our guy, our main man again, addresses this in his second lecture in Book 2 of the Nicomachean Ethics. He says, Here’s the deal with philosophy and the good life. A lot of folks spend time collecting data, collecting beliefs, collecting ideas. But they don’t actually practice what these beliefs preach. They are like people who collect a lot of advice from physicians and then never follow it.

Your doctor says, “You need to get healthy. You need to stop eating so many fatty and sugary foods, and you need to exercise every day.” And I collect this, and I write about it on Twitter, but then I never actually do the thing, and then I’m shocked that I’m not healthy.

So many philosophers are like doctors who don’t exercise. They have studied the theory of the case pretty well, and it’s good that human beings have this kind of theoretical knowledge, but if you’re not willing to actually make this a way of life, you are not gonna receive the benefits of it.

And unfortunately, way too many professional philosophers and professional scholars generally are like the doctors who aren’t willing to give up the sugary treats. They just collect all the data, but they don’t actually make it any part of how they care for their souls. So that’s not surprising.

That’s not to say we don’t want the data, we don’t wanna think about the ideas. It’s just to say the ideas get you, like, 20 percent of the way there. The rest of the 80 percent is actually trying to have a way of life.
